lessons.title: noir, blanc — one inherited, one borrowed
lessons.gloss: black and white — one word inherited from Latin, one borrowed from the Germanic neighbours

segments.text: Two colours, two completely different life stories. One walked straight down from Latin. The other was borrowed from the Germanic neighbours — and that direction, Germanic into Romance, is the opposite of what usually happens.
noir ("black") from Latin niger. No surprises: niger becomes negro/nero in the sister languages, and into English in denigrate ("to blacken someone's name").

You'd expect Latin albus ("white"). It's not there. French says blanc, from Frankish blank — a Germanic word meaning "shining, gleaming." The Franks who gave France its name gave it its word for white too.
Why did albus lose? Probably because blank was vivid: not just "white" but "bright, flashing." Colour words often get replaced by the more dramatic option.
It didn't die — it stopped being a colour:

utterances: word: aube. meaning: dawn. the white inside: the sky going white.
word: aubépine. meaning: hawthorn. the white inside: the "white thorn".
word: album (Eng.) meaning: album. the white inside: a blank white tablet.
word: albinos (Eng.) meaning: albino. the white inside: white-skinned.

segments.text: So Latin's white is still all around you — just never where you'd look for it.

segments.text: Which of the two is inherited from Latin? (Noir from niger.) Where does blanc come from? (Frankish blank, "shining" — a Germanic word borrowed into French.) Why is that direction surprising? (Latin usually lends to Germanic, not the other way.) Where did Latin albus end up? (In aube, "dawn," and album — no longer a colour.) Next: red and blue, and one more borrowing.

lessons.title: rouge, bleu — an ancient word and a borrowed one
lessons.gloss: red and blue — one ancient inherited root, and a second Germanic loan

segments.text: Last lesson: one inherited colour, one borrowed. This lesson repeats the pattern — and shows that French's borrowing from Germanic wasn't a one-off.
rouge from Latin rubeus ("reddish"). But rubeus itself descends from a root so old it predates Latin: PIE h₁rewdʰ-. Its children are everywhere:

utterances: language: Latin. word: ruber, rubeus becomes rouge, ruby, rubric.
language: English. word: red, rust, ruddy.

segments.text: So rouge and red are not lookalikes — they are actual cousins, separated for maybe five thousand years. Red is one of humanity's oldest named colours.

bleu from Frankish blāo. Another Germanic word, borrowed exactly like blanc. And then something neat happened: English took bleu from French — so English blue is a Germanic word that went to France, changed clothes, and came back. German kept the original at home: blau.
French also has azur (from the same source as Spanish azul, ultimately Arabic lāzaward, "lapis lazuli") — the poetic blue of the sky, and the Côte d'Azur.

utterances: colour: rouge. source: Latin rubeus (ancient PIE root).

segments.text: Half of French's basic colour vocabulary walked in from the north.

segments.text: What are rouge and English red to each other? (Cousins — both from PIE h₁rewdʰ-.) Where does bleu come from? (Germanic blāo — the second Germanic colour loan.) What did English do with it? (Borrowed it back from French as blue.) What are the three flag colours? (Bleu, blanc, rouge — and two of the three are loanwords.)
